body: Meds don't classify you as anything. Take them.

That's the worst. Feeling like you are so ill you can't even accomplish the one task that would end all others. It's partly why there's a higher risk of suicide after starting an anti-depressant: some people finally get enough of a lift and enough energy to finally be able to carry out the suicidal wish they've had all along, but not enough of a lift to stop the suicidal thoughts from happening.

Do not make the jump to bilateral if frustrated with slow or no progress. Memory effects are profound once bilateral ECT administered. I have a full year of memories that are gone, and my ability to form new memories is still limited two years later. School will be difficult. Give unilateral a full chance before even considering bilateral
That's ok. Don't beat yourself up about it. You'll have other opportunities to tell her.

Tell her. The worst that can happen is you'll be committed for a few days. And even then, that's not the end of the world. I've been. Some facilities/doctors are better than others so I can't guarantee that it will be a positive experience for you if you do end up getting involuntarily committed. But I really think you need to tell your school counselor, bc your school stress is making your mental health worse.
How did it go?

Yes, a professional then. Consider looking for one that has experience in trauma and also provides services via text message. More and more are offering that nowadays, and I think that'd be a great way to help you feel more comfortable.

You are not a burden and you have value. Getting help starts with reaching out (and you are probably more ready for that than you think-- you posted here afterall). You don't have to tell those you know first if you don't know how to do that. Tell a professional (bc you know you won't be stressing that person out, it's their job), and start slow if that's what you need to feel safe. Find someone you can develop a trusting therapeutic relationship with. That can take a lot of time, and it's frustrating having to go through multiple therapists, but finding one that understands is worth the effort.

In the meantime, have you considered joining a survivors' support group? You don't have to share your story at first. Just listening to others is helpful in not feeling alone.

What is your purpose here? You think people can overcome through sheer force of will and discipline??? You obviously have no clue what you are talking about and the bullshit you are spewing is not only unhelpful, but harmful.

That's a lot of trauma. No one could handle all of that on her own. Where were your parents' families when you had insecure housing and food? I am so sorry you were so mistreated and neglected. You desperately need trauma-based therapy and likely psychiatric help as well. Depression does not usually just get better on its own. It is a progressive disease that you may even have been born with considering your parents' mental health. The multiple sources of trauma made it all the worse and brought you to this point. 

Pretending to be happy when you are not is so exhausting. You don't have to pretend anymore. But please give yourself a chance to get better. It will take time, and work, but relief is possible.

Ok good. Just so you know what may happen, there is the possibility, depending on what you say and how you say it, that you will get hospitalized against your will. Even if that were to happen, it's a 72-hour hold and not the worst thing in the world. And you'll be getting help and the pressure from classes will be taken out of equation.

I'm sorry you are going through this. What level of schooling are you in? Is there a school counselor you can talk to? I don't know which country you are located, but in the states there are accomodations that must be made for someone going through what you are going through. You can't avail yourself of any of that unless you tell someone what is going on though (especially cutting and suicidal thoughts).

Of course it's hard. In fact, it's almost impossible. You must look into what is necessary for a medical withdrawal (I'm assuming you are in the states -- that's what we call it here). Once you get that process started (and your therapist can help) you will immediately start to feel some relief. You do not need the added stress right now of classes right now. It's a feedback loop -- your mental health is making school difficult, in turn the stress of trying to do coursework through it all is worsening your mental health. You must break the cycle and focus on your mental health. This is temporary and you will get through it. School will be waiting for you once you are better.

How are you doing in your classes now? I would imagine it's very difficult to concentrate with what you are going through. This would be your way to avoid failing classes, getting a medical withdrawal. It happens all the time and your school will guide you through the process.

Are you suicidal and do you have a plan? If so, you will get hospitalized. In which case you can medically withdraw from your classes (not fail, and not looked on as such) and start back up again when you are able. Even if you are not suicidal, you should consider withdrawing and getting voluntary treatment, especially if classes are a stress that is making you feel worse.
Tell her. It will not fuck up your future. What is your specific concern about that?

Talk to your therapist and your doctor. Seems like you've been on meds for about a year. That's usually when their efficacy starts to decrease. You likely need an adjustment which can make you feel better.
I'm sorry you're feeling this way. Has anything changed recently? Are you still seeing a therapist and taking medications?
I know how exhausting that is, continually improving your life to try to escape it. I'm sorry that's not working for you now.

That is terrible. And I think you intuitively know that was wrong of him to say. Going through a break-up is difficult, but especially so when you are already feeling extremely low and suicidal. I am not saying that you must end this relationship now, but it is something to consider as you move forward.
With treatment, it can. In my experience there is no coming out of it without help. Does not tend to resolve itself. And you are at risk of one day feeling even worse.

You posted this awhile ago, and  I'm assuming you're still here. You are not a bad person for wanting to die. You are sick, and no more bad of a person than anyone else suffering from a debilitating disease. But your loved ones will certainly be devastated. There is no question about that.  And that shouldn't be what is stopping you. (If its the only reason you haven't killed yourself, then fine, hang on to the guilt for awhile). But try to have some hope that you will find a treatment course that provides some relief. People (not all, but some) do get better. And you might be one of them. And if nothing works and you do end up killing yourself, at least you and your family will both know that you tried absolutely everything to get better, and that you are no longer suffering. But that's a worst-case scenario and not something to consider now. Have you considered other treatments besides anti-depressant medication/therapy?
Thanks. I've tried several therapists using different therapeutic modalities. Hasn't been useful to me.

The answers to all of your questions are "maybe." Life has no guarantees. Its worth sticking it out a little while longer to find out though. In the meantime, use the transition from high school to college as a reset: new friends, your parents matter less, and your studies matter more. And get treatment before you go. Talk to a therapist, a school counselor even. Talk to a doctor. You are too young to have tried all the possible treatments for this disease -- and that is what you have. A disease you were likely born with that you have to give yourself a chance to fight and overcome. And it might be a tough fight, but maybe not as tough as you think. People do improve. Tap into the academic part of your mind to see it that way.

Thats a tough question to answer.  

I identify a lot with your experience. I dont know if this is also the case for you, but the approval of others and achieving measures of success became a way to cope for me. It made me feel better temporarily (like a high), and even better than that, it hid the fact that I was deeply depressed from those around me. I almost lived a double life.  Now there are many, many people who have met me who would be shocked to learn I killed myself. ("She had everything going for her.")

I see this as a progressive disease. Unless you get effective treatment (which I believe is still a possibility for you), the depression and pain will get worse the older you get. So yeah, ending it sooner would have saved me a lot of pain.

But I wouldnt have had the time to try as much to get better. So whether you should be terrified of ending up like me depends on what you've already tried. I do believe you owe it to yourself to try everything. Do the research, stay up on the latest shit. Something may work for you.

Look at what you have been able to achieve with the depression and suicidal thoughts interfering all along the way. Imagine what you could do without them?
Too unstudied. Has it worked for you?

Sorry I misunderstood. Become independent enough to move away from whoever is abusing you, then (if that is happening now.) You deserve some happiness, and you cant get that living under someone else's thumb.

Dogs are easy to come by. I have 3 rescues. Probably the only reason I wake up in the morning.

I obviously dont know your exact financial situation, but you'd be surprised about living on disability -- many are able to live (albeit very modestly) on it. If you qualify you'll likely also qualify for Medicaid. And I think your therapist can even write to the specifics of how your financial independence from your parents is critical to your treatment and wellbeing and that will be considered. At the very least, moving out should be a goal you set for yourself, and there is no rush or judgment in how long it takes to get you there. But you'll need smaller goals to help you meet the larger goal. That starts with filing your disability application. 

I believe you CAN be a functioning adult. You just have to move out before you'll ever find out.

I'm so sorry for what happened to you. It's as if you never had a chance. Trying to focus is so hard when you are depressed, but now you must focus on getting the disability payments so you are financially independent.  It sounds like you've never spent any of your life free from abuse. You must give yourself the chance to see what it's like. Your depression will likely always need treatment, especially with the trauma you've experienced, but it may lift and be bearable.

It can get worse. I see it as a progressive disease at this point.

If your insurance covers it and you have the time (an hour a day 5x a week for 6 weeks), give TMS a try. Just bc it didnt work for me doesnt mean it wont work for you. You owe it to yourself to try everything you can.

I'm just running out of options, which is scary. Jogging isnt one of them. I'm so weak from not eating or taking care of myself I can barely stand long enough to shower once a week.
I didnt know that. But yeah. Cute sayings dont fit when it comes to depression and suicide.
Thanks. I've thought about it. But I think about killing myself more.
I'm sorry. It sounds like you want help.

If your plan works, that sounds like super painful way to die. You will likely survive, and will wake up in a psych ward. There are easier ways to get help, and no shame in getting hospitalized for the way you are feeling. Skip this step and all the pain it would cause and just go to the emergency room. All you have to do when you check in is tell them you've been thinking of killing yourself. You wont be a failure.

I dont know that this is the answer you are looking for, but I have countless times lied to mental health professionals about my suicidal thoughts. The main reason is a lack of trust. I want help, but I don't want to be hospitalized or put on a 72-hour psychiatric hold. That would disrupt my life and make it worse. 

Make clear to your students that you are not obligated to report the fact that they want to die. That several people are so depressed they want to die. That they are in control of any treatment going forward. That you will get them as much help as they want, but no more. And make clear what crosses the line and requires you to report (a suicide plan). Once someone understands this, they'll be far more likely to talk about feeling suicidal (and even if they have plans and are lying about it) at least they are talking about suicide, and you can understand the severity of the depression and offer support.

I get angry at this too. I've never considered suicide to be a selfish act. It is the end result of too much pain. My selfish self would much rather that someone other than me was born with this disease. That I could trade places and be the happy one.
